Nx s1ngularity exfiltration: public GitHub repo named 's1ngularity-repository' or results.b64 commit AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the distinctive exfil pattern used by the Nx s1ngularity npm compromise — the postinstall payload creates a *public* GitHub repository in the victim's own namespace called s1ngularity-repository (sometimes with numeric suffixes) and pushes a base64-encoded results.b64 file. Catches the network/file-system side of the same chain. Rationale: Article names Nx s1ngularity as a postinstall-script credential stealer that 'uploaded credentials to public GitHub repos'. External sources (Kodem, Ox Security, Endor Labs) confirm the specific repo-name convention 's1ngularity-repository' and the base64-encoded results.b64 commit payload — both are deterministic, distinctive strings unlikely to appear in benign telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.kodemsecurity.com/resources/vulnerability-alert-s1ngularity-malicious-nx-npm-packages • https://www.ox.security/blog/nx-supply-chain-breach-how-s1ngularity-weaponized-ai/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/learnings-from-recent-npm-compromises/
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1041 T1132.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR/research analyst replaying the s1ngularity payload in a sandbox VM also in EDR scope
  • Internal red-team exercise simulating the s1ngularity worm
  • Security-research repo legitimately named with 's1ngularity' for documentation
  • Threat-intel feed ingestion tooling that downloads sample artifacts named results.b64
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the parent process is node/npm/bun chain (true positive) versus a known sandbox host; pull the offending npm install command line to identify the compromised package + version. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the developer host, immediately delete the public s1ngularity-repository from the victim's GitHub namespace (treat as already-indexed by adversaries — assume secrets stolen), revoke every credential the user could touch, and rotate. Step 3 — Hunt: query GitHub audit log org-wide for recent public-repo creation events with 's1ngularity' or 'results.b64' commit messages, sweep file telemetry for all hosts touching the same SHA256, and check npm publish events for any package this developer maintains downstream.
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let FileArtifacts =
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where FileName =~ "results.b64"
         or FolderPath has "s1ngularity-repository"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
              Indicator=strcat("file:", FolderPath, "\\", FileName),
              ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let NetworkArtifacts =
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","bun.exe","node","npm","yarn","pnpm","bun","curl.exe","wget.exe","git.exe")
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com/user/repos","api.github.com/repos","github.com/")
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("s1ngularity","results.b64","repos?per_page","\"private\":false")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
              Indicator=strcat("net:", RemoteUrl),
              ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
union FileArtifacts, NetworkArtifacts
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let FileArtifacts =
    ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where TargetFileName =~ "results.b64"
         or TargetFilePath has "s1ngularity-repository"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
              Indicator=strcat("file:", TargetFilePath),
              ParentCmd=ActingProcessCommandLine;
let NetworkArtifacts =
    ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where Url has_any ("api.github.com/user/repos","api.github.com/repos")
    | where HttpMethod in ("POST","PUT","PATCH")
    | where HttpRequestBodyBytes > 0
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername=SrcUsername,
              Indicator=strcat("net:", Url),
              ParentCmd=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent;
union FileArtifacts, NetworkArtifacts
| order by TimeGenerated desc

node-gyp implicit rebuild via binding.gyp spawning unexpected non-build child processes AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the binding.gyp implicit code-execution path the article calls out as a sleeper vector — npm runs an implicit `node-gyp rebuild` for any package containing a binding.gyp even when the scripts field is empty. Surface node-gyp/node spawning anything outside the legitimate compiler/linker toolchain. Rationale: Article calls out binding.gyp as a sleeper execution vector: 'a package ships a binding.gyp, npm runs an implicit node-gyp rebuild for it during install, so a dependency with a spotless package.json can still execute code'. This UC anchors on that exact path — node-gyp parent + non-toolchain child = code running outside the documented scripts field. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/npm-v12-block-postinstall
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Esoteric native modules with custom build helpers (e.g. node-canvas calling Python to find pkg-config)
  • Modules using node-pre-gyp to download prebuilt binaries via curl/wget
  • Internal native modules that shell out to ImageMagick/ffmpeg as part of build
  • Cross-compilation toolchain dispatch scripts not in the allowlist
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-canvas","node-pre-gyp","prebuild-install") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("http://","-EncodedCommand","base64","IEX"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: read the parent node-gyp command line to identify the package name and version doing the rebuild, then read the suspect package's binding.gyp + any referenced .py/.js build script to determine if the child invocation is documented. Step 2 — Contain: if the child binary or downloaded URL is unrecognised, isolate the host and treat the developer's environment as compromised — rotate npm/GitHub/SSH/cloud credentials. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot fleet-wide on the package name + version via DeviceFileEvents, examine all node-gyp rebuilds from the same package across other developers, and check npm registry for the package's other recent versions for sibling binding.gyp changes.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let BuildToolchain = dynamic(["cl.exe","link.exe","lib.exe","mc.exe","rc.exe","midl.exe","python.exe","python3","python","make","gmake","gcc","g++","clang","clang++","ld","ar","ranlib","strip","nm","as","node.exe","node","conhost.exe","vcvarsall.bat","msbuild.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp rebuild","node-gyp configure","binding.gyp")
     or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node-gyp.exe","node-gyp")
| where FileName !in~ (BuildToolchain)
| where FileName !endswith ".tmp"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildSHA256 = SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let BuildToolchain = dynamic(["cl.exe","link.exe","lib.exe","mc.exe","rc.exe","midl.exe","python.exe","python3","python","make","gmake","gcc","g++","clang","clang++","ld","ar","ranlib","strip","nm","as","node.exe","node","conhost.exe","vcvarsall.bat","msbuild.exe"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp rebuild","node-gyp configure","binding.gyp")
     or ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)[\\/]node-gyp(\.exe)?$"
| extend ChildBase = tolower(tostring(split(TargetProcessName, "/")[-1]))
| extend ChildBaseWin = tolower(tostring(split(TargetProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where not(ChildBase in (BuildToolchain) or ChildBaseWin in (BuildToolchain))
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentImage = ParentProcessName,
          ParentCmd   = ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = TargetProcessName,
          ChildCmd    = ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildSHA256 = SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("142.11.206.73") or RemoteUrl has_any ("sfrclak.com", "webhook.site")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["142.11.206.73"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["sfrclak.com", "webhook.site"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("142.11.206.73")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("sfrclak.com", "webhook.site")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("sfrclak.com", "webhook.site")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("142.11.206.73")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("sfrclak.com", "webhook.site")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("sfrclak.com", "webhook.site")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]

or MD5 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "b74caeaa75e077c99f7d44f46daaf9796a3be43ecf24f2a1fd381844669da777",         | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "b74caeaa75e077c99f7d44f46daaf9796a3be43ecf24f2a1fd381844669da777", "dc67467a39b70d1cd4c1f7f7a459b35058163592f4a9e8fb4dffcbba98ef210c", "4b2399646573bb737c4969563303d8ee2e9ddbd1b271f1ca9e35ea78062538db", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Vulnerable meta-ads-mcp version (≤1.0.108) inventoried on host · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Unauthenticated POST /mcp to meta-ads-mcp on default port 8080
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-48039: Meta Ads MCP: Unauthenticated HTTP MCP Tool Ex
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] FastAPI/Starlette uvicorn on port 8080 hosting meta-ads-mcp without auth dependency
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] meta-ads-mcp process exfiltrating to graph.facebook.com without prior OAuth handshake
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Meta access_token leaked in JSON-RPC response body from MCP /mcp endpoint · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Unauthenticated POST /mcp to meta-ads-mcp on default port 8080 AIDelivery High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP POST requests to the /mcp endpoint of pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp (CVE-2026-48039). The AuthInjectionMiddleware.dispatch() at http_auth_integration.py:272 falls through to call_next without returning 401, allowing any network-reachable caller to invoke MCP tools as the operator. Rationale: Article names the exact vulnerable port (8080), endpoint (/mcp), HTTP method (POST), and package (pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp ≤1.0.108). Any unauthenticated POST to /mcp on this port is the literal exploit primitive at http_auth_integration.py:272. Cross-checked GitHub advisory GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48039
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate authenticated MCP client (Claude Desktop, Cursor) calling /mcp with valid Authorization header
  • Internal security scanner (Burp / nuclei) probing /mcp during sanctioned pentest
  • Health-check probe from container orchestrator (k8s livenessProbe) hitting /mcp
  • Developer running curl against localhost:8080 during local debugging
  • Pipeboard.co session-token flow that uses X-Pipeboard-Token instead of Authorization
Suppression filter
and not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Claude-Desktop","Cursor","ModelContextProtocol","kube-probe") and SourceIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Confirm SourceIP is external/untrusted. Pull the full HTTP request: was Authorization or X-Pipeboard-Token header present? Check the meta-ads-mcp version on the target host (pip show meta-ads-mcp). Step 2 — Contain: If unauthenticated and external, block SourceIP at the perimeter, take the meta-ads-mcp container offline (docker stop / kubectl delete pod), and rotate META_ACCESS_TOKEN at developers.facebook.com immediately — assume token is compromised. Step 3 — Hunt: Search 30 days of proxy/WAF logs for the same SourceIP hitting /mcp anywhere in the estate; pivot on the META_ACCESS_TOKEN to find outbound graph.facebook.com calls not originating from your server (indicates attacker is using the stolen token).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ConnectionSuccess")
| where LocalPort == 8080
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python.exe","python3","uvicorn.exe","gunicorn","meta-ads-mcp")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta_ads_mcp","meta-ads-mcp","http_auth_integration")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 8080
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/mcp"
| where EventOutcome in~ ("200","201","Success")
| where isempty(RequestCookies) or RequestCookies !has "auth"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, RequestCookies, EventOutcome, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Meta access_token leaked in JSON-RPC response body from MCP /mcp endpoint AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential exfiltration primitive of CVE-2026-48039: api.py:263–269 serialises the raw httpx request_url containing access_token=… as a query parameter into the 200 OK JSON-RPC response, delivering the operator's META_ACCESS_TOKEN to the caller verbatim on any Graph API error path. Rationale: Article quotes the literal leak path: request_url field containing access_token=FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO_123456789 in the 200 OK JSON-RPC response. The regex anchors on the exact pattern api.py:136 produces (access_token query parameter). Cross-checked GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr • https://github.com/pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer pasting an example access_token=… string into a legitimate debug response
  • Authenticated MCP client receiving a sanitised error that retained the access_token field name without value
  • TLS-inspecting WAF logging a benign /graph endpoint's response where access_token is also in a downstream caller's body
  • Pen-test tooling (Burp Collaborator) deliberately echoing access_token strings to validate the bug
  • Internal smoke test for the patched version (1.0.109+) that intentionally exercises the old code path
Suppression filter
and not (Message has "redacted" or Message has "REDACTED" or LeakedToken matches regex @"FAKE|EXAMPLE|TEST|XXXX")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Capture the leaked token string and check Meta Business Suite audit logs for activity using that token. Confirm whether the token is the operator's META_ACCESS_TOKEN env var on the host. Step 2 — Contain: Immediately rotate the leaked Meta access token at developers.facebook.com → My Apps → Access Tokens; revoke all sessions for the associated Meta Business account. Take the vulnerable meta-ads-mcp container offline. Step 3 — Hunt: Search EDR for outbound HTTPS to graph.facebook.com NOT originating from the legitimate meta-ads-mcp host — that indicates the attacker is reusing the token. Pull 90 days of Meta Ads API activity for unauthorised ad spend, account changes, or pixel/audience exfiltration.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where LocalPort == 8080
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta_ads_mcp","meta-ads-mcp","http_auth_integration","uvicorn")
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ConnectionSuccess")
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has "graph.facebook.com" or RemoteUrl has "graph.instagram.com"
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta_ads_mcp","meta-ads-mcp")
  ) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, LocalPort, RemoteUrl1, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 8080
| where RequestURL has "/mcp"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where Message has "access_token=" or Message has "request_url" or Message has "graph.facebook.com"
| extend LeakedToken = extract(@"access_token=([A-Za-z0-9_\-]{20,})", 1, Message)
| where isnotempty(LeakedToken)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, EventOutcome, LeakedToken, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

meta-ads-mcp process exfiltrating to graph.facebook.com without prior OAuth handshake AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the downstream exfil path of CVE-2026-48039 — once the operator's META_ACCESS_TOKEN is stolen via /mcp, attackers reuse it directly against graph.facebook.com. Flags meta-ads-mcp (or its host process) connecting to Meta Graph endpoints from unexpected hosts or in unusual volumes. Rationale: Article explicitly states the exfil destination: 'https://graph.facebook.com/v24.0/me/adaccounts'. Hosts running meta-ads-mcp legitimately hit graph.facebook.com; the detection inverts that to find OTHER hosts in the estate suddenly making the same calls (attacker reusing stolen token). Cross-checked GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr and CVE-2026-48039. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr • https://developers.facebook.com/docs/marketing-api/
ATT&CKT1041 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Marketing team workstation legitimately running Meta Ads Manager browser app
  • Internal CI/CD job using Meta Marketing API SDK for ad reporting
  • Mobile-developer host running Facebook SDK debugger
  • Web analytics tool resolving Facebook pixel domains
  • Personal-use of Facebook from a BYOD host visible to corp DNS
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Identify the process / user driving the connection on the non-MCP host. Check if the user has any legitimate Meta Ads role. Pull the Meta Business audit log for the access_token used. Step 2 — Contain: Rotate the META_ACCESS_TOKEN immediately; revoke Meta Business sessions; block egress to graph.facebook.com from the suspect host. Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot on the suspect host's external IP to find all inbound /mcp traffic to your meta-ads-mcp servers (same source IP that stole the token will likely have probed it). Audit Meta Ad accounts for unauthorised campaigns, pixel changes, or audience exports in the last 30 days.

Vulnerable meta-ads-mcp version (≤1.0.108) inventoried on host AIReconnaissance High
Identifies hosts running pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp versions ≤1.0.108 (the patched-or-not boundary per the advisory). 1.0.102–1.0.105 are explicitly flagged as 'patch status unconfirmed' because they lack git tags. Asset-inventory pivot for CVE-2026-48039 exposure scoping. Rationale: Article gives the exact affected version range: 'Affected packages: pip:meta-ads-mcp (vuln <= 1.0.108)' and calls out 1.0.102–1.0.105 as patch-status-unconfirmed because they lack git tags. Detection enumerates installed versions to scope exposure. Cross-checked GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr • https://pypi.org/project/meta-ads-mcp/
ATT&CKT1518.001 T1592.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer sandbox intentionally running the vulnerable build to test the patch
  • Air-gapped lab box without network exposure (vulnerable but unreachable)
  • Container image rebuilt to a later version but inventory cache not refreshed (false positive — patched in reality)
  • meta-ads-mcp installed but daemon not running (no listener, not exploitable)
  • Pip dev install (-e) showing as version 0.0.0 — needs manual version pin check
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: For each affected host, confirm meta-ads-mcp HTTP listener is actually bound to a network interface (netstat -ant | grep 8080) — air-gapped/loopback-only installs are not exploitable. Step 2 — Contain: Upgrade to pip install --upgrade meta-ads-mcp (≥1.0.109 once published) OR firewall the host's port 8080 from untrusted networks AND switch from META_ACCESS_TOKEN env var to per-request Authorization: Bearer pattern per advisory remediation. Step 3 — Hunt: For every host on the list, run UC-1 and UC-2 (unauthenticated /mcp POST and token-leak detection) retrospectively over 90 days to determine if the vuln was already exploited.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "meta-ads-mcp" or SoftwareName has "meta_ads_mcp" or SoftwareName has "pipeboard"

FastAPI/Starlette uvicorn on port 8080 hosting meta-ads-mcp without auth dependency AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the execution-side root cause of CVE-2026-48039: python uvicorn (or gunicorn) serving the meta-ads-mcp Starlette ASGI app on port 8080. Combines process command-line for uvicorn + listener on 8080 + meta_ads_mcp module load — the exact runtime shape the advisory describes. Rationale: Article names the exact runtime: Starlette ASGI middleware (AuthInjectionMiddleware.dispatch) in http_auth_integration.py, served on default port 8080 per the PoC docker command. Detection pins on the python+uvicorn/gunicorn+meta_ads_mcp triple — the vulnerable runtime shape. Cross-checked GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr • https://github.com/pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Patched 1.0.109+ build running the same uvicorn+meta_ads_mcp combo (now safe — needs version cross-check)
  • Local developer test instance bound to 127.0.0.1 only (not externally exploitable)
  • Container scan job loading the package metadata without running the server
  • CI test job spinning the server up briefly to run unit tests then tearing down
  • meta-ads-mcp used in stdio mode (no HTTP listener) — different transport not affected
Suppression filter
and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--host 127.0.0.1","--host localhost","-h 127.0.0.1") or InitiatingProcessFileName in ("pytest.exe","pytest","tox.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: For each match, check the bound interface (lsof -i :8080 / netstat -plnt | grep 8080) — loopback-only is safe, 0.0.0.0 / public IP is exposed. Pull the meta-ads-mcp version from the same host (pip show meta-ads-mcp). Step 2 — Contain: For exposed hosts running ≤1.0.108: stop the daemon (systemctl stop / docker stop / kill the python PID), upgrade the package, rotate META_ACCESS_TOKEN. For exposed hosts running 1.0.102–1.0.105: assume vulnerable until proven patched (advisory says git tags missing). Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot on each confirmed-vulnerable host's external IP into /mcp access logs to confirm whether unauthenticated callers reached it during the exposure window.

Miasma worm GitHub commit-search C2 magic strings on command line or script AICommand & Control High
Hunts for the three hard-coded GitHub commit-search query strings the Miasma supply-chain worm uses as its three independent C2 channels (PAT discovery, JavaScript payload delivery, Python payload delivery). These strings have zero legitimate business presence and are the highest-fidelity Miasma indicator available. Rationale: The three strings 'DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom', 'TheBeautifulSandsOfTime' and 'firedalazer' are the hard-coded GitHub commit-search queries each Miasma C2 channel uses (PAT discovery, JS payload, Python payload). They are confirmed by SafeDep's analysis, BleepingComputer's report, and a parallel TheHackerNews write-up. Zero legitimate business processes contain these tokens. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-supply-chain-attack-compromises.html • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002 T1059.007 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst running these strings through their own grep/search tooling for hunting
  • SOC engineer pasting the IOCs into a script or note file
  • Security researcher cloning or reading SafeDep / Cloudsmith write-ups in a developer IDE that logs URL paths
  • Sandbox / detonation environment intentionally executing a Miasma sample for analysis
  • Automation that ingests OSS-supply-chain advisories and writes IOCs to a database column
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("misp.exe","opencti.exe") and not (FolderPath has_any ("\\sandbox\\","\\detonation\\","\\analyst-tools\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process that emitted the string is not an analyst hunting tool, a CTI ingestion script, or a known sandbox. Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain; if the string was in a network URL, identify what process issued the GET against api.github.com/search/commits. 2) Contain: if the originating process is a node/python/git/curl invocation on a developer machine or CI runner, isolate the host from network, revoke any GitHub PATs and SSH keys cached on it, and rotate npm/PyPI/RubyGems publish tokens and JFrog Artifactory credentials owned by that user. 3) Hunt: search 30d for the same three strings org-wide; pivot on the parent process and SHA256 to find sibling executions; review the developer's git push history for npm/PyPI/RubyGems package versions published in the last 7d for unexpected new releases or postinstall scripts.
let MiasmaC2 = dynamic(["DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, Source = "Process";
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","github.com")
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName = InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256 = InitiatingProcessSHA256, Source = strcat("Net:", RemoteUrl);
union ProcHits, NetHits
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaC2 = dynamic(["DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
let From4688 = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source = "4688";
let FromAsim = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2) or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, NewProcessName = TargetProcessName, CommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName, Source = "ASIM";
union From4688, FromAsim
| where Account !endswith "$"
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma supply-chain worm leaked repo clone, install or fetch AIDelivery High
Hunts for git clone / npm install / pip install / curl / wget operations that reference the briefly-public 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release' GitHub repositories which leaked the worm's source on 2026-06-08. A match means the host has either ingested the leaked toolkit or is being staged with it. Rationale: 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release' is the exact repository slug SafeDep and BleepingComputer report appeared on GitHub from 2026-06-08 hosting the leaked toolkit. The string is uniquely tied to Miasma and would only surface in dev-tool command lines or proxy URLs when a host is cloning, installing or downloading the leaked source. Cross-checked via SafeDep, BleepingComputer and TheRegister. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074 • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1105 T1588.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel team intentionally cloning the leaked repo into a sandbox for analysis
  • Security researcher fetching the source on a developer workstation for write-up
  • SOAR / TIP ingesting OSS advisory feeds and storing the repo URL as an IOC string
  • Vulnerability scanner or SCA tool fingerprinting against known-malicious repo names
  • Blue-team CTF or training environment seeding the toolkit deliberately
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\detonation\\", "\\malware-analysis\\", "\\threat-intel\\") and FolderPath !has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\detonation\\", "\\malware-analysis\\", "\\threat-intel\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user and parent process that issued the clone/install/fetch — confirm it is not a sanctioned analyst sandbox or CTI ingestion job. Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and any subsequent npm/pip postinstall script execution from the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node/python child processes spawned within 1 hour of the clone, revoke GitHub PATs and SSH keys cached on it, and rotate npm/PyPI/RubyGems/Artifactory publish tokens belonging to the user. 3) Hunt: search 30d for the three Miasma C2 commit-search strings (see related UC) on the same host and across the org; review the user's recent package publishes for unexpected versions; check GitHub Actions workflows in any repo they touched for newly-added steps referencing untrusted secrets or external scripts.
let MiasmaRepo = "Miasma-Open-Source-Release";
let DevTools = dynamic(["git.exe","npm.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","git","npm","node","pip","python","python3","curl","wget"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ (DevTools) or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (DevTools)
    | where ProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo or InitiatingProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, Source = "Process";
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl contains MiasmaRepo
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "Network";
union isfuzzy=true ProcHits, NetHits
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaRepo = "Miasma-Open-Source-Release";
let From4688 = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source = "4688";
let FromAsim = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo or TargetProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, NewProcessName = TargetProcessName, CommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName, Source = "ASIM";
let FromProxy = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL contains MiasmaRepo or DestinationHostName contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = SourceHostName, Account = SourceUserName, NewProcessName = "", CommandLine = RequestURL, ParentProcessName = "", Source = "Proxy";
union From4688, FromAsim, FromProxy
| where Account !endswith "$"
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.

Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FireAnt Metakit supply-chain: update binary spawning unusual child
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — OceanLotus: From external espionage to domestic targeting
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SPECTRALVIPER known-sample SHA1 execution or filesystem write · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C2 connection to ESET-disclosed IPs/domains · [LLM] First-seen connection to recently-registered SPECTRALVIPER-shape C2 domain · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C2 connection to ESET-disclosed IPs/domains AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any outbound network connection to the eight SPECTRALVIPER C2 IPs and six C&C domains ESET published for OceanLotus's 2024-2026 FireAnt Metakit supply-chain and Vietnamese construction-corp campaigns. High-fidelity because every IOC is a known-bad C2 endpoint with no documented benign use. Rationale: Every IP and domain in this query is a SPECTRALVIPER C&C endpoint published in ESET's Table 2 and IOC bundle for the 2024-2026 OceanLotus campaigns; financemachinelearning.com is explicitly named as the C&C domain for the stable SPECTRALVIPER variant. Match by IP catches direct fallback; match by URL catches HTTPS proxied through hostname.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox / malware-analysis VM intentionally detonating SPECTRALVIPER samples
  • Threat-intel scrapers / Shodan-style researchers actively probing the IOC set
  • Security-tool URL-categorization scans of the malicious domains (e.g. Zscaler, Netskope)
  • Legitimate hosts that happen to be on a shared-IP CDN that now resolves to one of these IPs (rare — most IOCs are bare hosting)
  • DNS sinkhole responses if these domains have been sinkholed by a TI provider
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\" or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","iexplore.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the full process tree from DeviceProcessEvents for InitiatingProcessFileName at the time of the connection — confirm whether the originator is a known good binary (security tooling, sandbox) or an unsigned binary in a temp/AppData path matching SPECTRALVIPER drop patterns. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the device via Defender Live Response or EDR network-isolation, block the matched IP/domain at firewall and EDR network indicator policy, force credential reset for the InitiatingProcessAccountName. 3) HUNT: pivot on DeviceFileEvents for SHA1 against the 20-hash IOC set; query DnsEvents for the other five C&C domains across all hosts in the last 90 days; search for any FireAnt Metakit installs (file path or process name) on neighboring hosts and check their update history for a malicious payload window of Oct-2025 to Mar-2026.

let ioc_domains = dynamic(["financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com","coachcybersecurity.com","mxprodesign.com","power-sync-services.com","leadingfilipinoteams.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where RemoteIP in (ioc_ips) or RemoteUrl has_any (ioc_domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

SPECTRALVIPER known-sample SHA1 execution or filesystem write AIInstallation High
Alerts whenever a process executes or a file is written whose SHA1 matches one of the 20 SPECTRALVIPER / OceanLotus stager and dropper hashes ESET published. Covers both SPECTRALVIPER backdoor binaries and the malicious FireAnt Metakit update payloads from the supply-chain wave. Rationale: All 20 SHA1s are pulled directly from the IOC block of the ESET report and correspond to SPECTRALVIPER samples (both old reused first-iteration samples and fresh stable-version samples from Table 1) plus the FireAnt Metakit supply-chain droppers. Hash match on process + filesystem + image-load catches dropper, persistent loader, and DLL side-load variants.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1027 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Defender / CrowdStrike sample-submission VMs ingesting the IOC bundle for testing
  • DFIR teams replaying confirmed malware samples during tabletop exercises
  • VirusTotal / hybrid-analysis collector hosts that store hash archives
  • Security researcher endpoints reverse-engineering the samples
  • Backup/restore restoring a previously-quarantined sample from shadow copy
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "malware" and DeviceName !has "detonation"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify whether the host is a known malware-analysis sandbox or a production endpoint — check device tags, OU membership and the user profile of InitiatingProcessAccountName. If production, this is a confirmed-malicious detection with no investigation needed before action. 2) CONTAIN: network-isolate the device, kill the process tree, quarantine the binary, force credential rotation for any account with an interactive logon to that host in the last 90 days, and block the SHA1 across the EDR fleet via Indicators of Compromise policy. 3) HUNT: for every host that ran one of these hashes, pull DeviceNetworkEvents and DnsEvents 30 days back looking for the six SPECTRALVIPER C2 domains and eight IPs; check FireAnt Metakit install history; pivot on the InitiatingProcessFolderPath to identify the dropper that wrote the sample.

FireAnt Metakit supply-chain: update binary spawning unusual child AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for the FireAnt Metakit application (the Vietnamese stock-investment platform whose update server OceanLotus compromised from Oct-2025 to Mar-2026) spawning script interpreters, LOLBins, or unsigned binaries from temp/AppData. This is the textbook detection shape for the supply-chain payload that ESET observed delivering SPECTRALVIPER after a poisoned update. Rationale: ESET explicitly names FireAnt Metakit as the compromised stock-trading platform and describes the update-server-replaced-with-malicious-payload pattern; any FireAnt Metakit process spawning a script interpreter, LOLBin, or binary out of temp/AppData is the operational shape of the supply-chain payload chain that ends in SPECTRALVIPER drop. Hunting tier because FireAnt's own update process may legitimately invoke some installer LOLBins on first install.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate FireAnt Metakit update invoking msiexec.exe during a real product update
  • FireAnt installer writing helper binaries to %TEMP% as part of normal first-run installation
  • Endpoint backup software (Veeam, Acronis) interacting with FireAnt install directory during scheduled backup
  • User troubleshooting FireAnt by running it from a portable/extracted location in Downloads
  • Antivirus / DLP scanning FireAnt binaries on a schedule and reading from AppData
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessSignatureStatus != "Valid" or ChildSHA256 !in~ (toscalar(DeviceFileCertificateInfo | where IsSigned == true and SignatureType == "CodeSign" | summarize make_set(SHA256)))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the FireAnt Metakit installer SHA256 and version from InitiatingProcessSHA256 / VersionInfoProductVersion and compare against the vendor's published known-good hash; check the timestamp against ESET's Oct-2025 to Mar-2026 supply-chain window — any install in that range is suspect by default. 2) CONTAIN: if the parent SHA256 is unknown or in the known-bad set, isolate the host, kill the process tree, and quarantine all files written by the child process in the prior 24h; alert the user to discontinue use of FireAnt Metakit pending vendor confirmation. 3) HUNT: query DeviceNetworkEvents on the host for any of the six SPECTRALVIPER C2 domains in the 7 days after the install; pivot DeviceFileEvents for files written by InitiatingProcessFolderPath of FireAnt to identify dropped stagers; check for any other endpoints in the org running FireAnt and audit their install times.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "fireant" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName has "fireant"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","msiexec.exe")
   or FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentSHA256 = InitiatingProcessSHA256,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildSHA256 = SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where ParentProcessName has "fireant" or ActingProcessName has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit") or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","msiexec.exe")
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA1, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
